courses.title: Nigerian Peoples and Culture (GST 112)
courses.description: General-studies course on Nigeria's peoples, history, government and culture, taken by all 100 Level students.

topics.title: The Land and Peoples of Nigeria
topics.summary: Geography, ethnic diversity, states and geopolitical zones of Nigeria.

material.heading: Geography and administration
material.body: Nigeria lies in West Africa on the Gulf of Guinea, bordered by Benin (west), Niger (north), Chad (north-east) and Cameroon (east). It has 36 states plus the Federal Capital Territory (Abuja) and 774 local government areas, grouped into six geopolitical zones: North-West, North-East, North-Central, South-West, South-East and South-South. Abuja replaced Lagos as the capital on 12 December 1991.

material.heading: Ethnic diversity
material.body: Nigeria has over 250 ethnic groups and more than 500 languages. The three largest groups are the Hausa-Fulani (north), Yoruba (south-west) and Igbo (south-east). Others include the Ijaw, Kanuri, Ibibio, Tiv, Edo, Nupe, Urhobo and Efik. The name 'Nigeria' was suggested by Flora Shaw (later Lady Lugard) in 1897, from the River Niger.
keyPoints: Hausa-Fulani, Yoruba and Igbo are the largest

topics.title: Pre-colonial States and Societies
topics.summary: Political organisation of the Oyo, Benin, Hausa, Kanem-Bornu and Igbo societies and the Sokoto Caliphate.

material.heading: Centralised states
material.body: The Oyo Empire was ruled by the Alaafin, checked by the Oyo Mesi (council of seven kingmakers led by the Bashorun) and the Ogboni society. The Benin Kingdom was headed by the Oba, with chiefs such as the Uzama. Kanem-Bornu, one of the oldest states, was ruled by the Mai and later the Shehu. The Hausa city-states (e.g. Kano, Katsina, Zaria) were led by Sarkis (Habe kings) until the Fulani jihad of Usman dan Fodio (from 1804) created the Sokoto Caliphate, governed by Emirs under the Sultan.
keyPoints: Oyo: Alaafin checked by Oyo Mesi and Ogboni

material.heading: Non-centralised (acephalous) societies
material.body: The Igbo and Tiv were largely decentralised. Igbo communities governed themselves through the council of elders, the Ofo title holders, age grades, the Umuada (married daughters) and title societies such as Ozo. Decisions were often reached by consensus in village assemblies. This structure later made British indirect rule difficult in the east, leading to the imposition of warrant chiefs and the Aba Women's Riot of 1929.
keyPoints: Igbo: republican, age grades, council of elders
Warrant chiefs led to the Aba Women's Riot (1929)

topics.title: Colonial Rule and Amalgamation
topics.summary: British conquest, amalgamation of 1914, indirect rule and the colonial constitutions.

material.heading: Amalgamation and indirect rule
material.body: Britain annexed Lagos in 1861, and after the Royal Niger Company's charter was revoked (1900) created the Protectorates of Northern and Southern Nigeria. On 1 January 1914 Sir Frederick Lugard amalgamated them into one colony and protectorate. Lugard's system of indirect rule governed through traditional rulers; it worked best in the emirate North, less well in the West, and failed in the East, where warrant chiefs were imposed.
keyPoints: Indirect rule succeeded most in the North

material.heading: Colonial constitutions
material.body: The Clifford Constitution (1922) introduced the elective principle, giving Lagos and Calabar elected members and stimulating party formation (Herbert Macaulay's NNDP, 1923). The Richards Constitution (1946) created regional houses of assembly; the Macpherson Constitution (1951) involved wider consultation; the Lyttelton Constitution (1954) made Nigeria a federation. Independence came on 1 October 1960, and Nigeria became a republic on 1 October 1963.

questions.explanation: Britain formally annexed Lagos in 1861.

questions.explanation: The 1946 Richards Constitution established regional assemblies.

topics.title: Independence, the Civil War and Nation Building
topics.summary: Post-independence politics, military rule, the civil war, and national unity institutions.

material.heading: From independence to civil war
material.body: At independence (1960) Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa was Prime Minister. The first military coup occurred on 15 January 1966, bringing Major-General Aguiyi-Ironsi to power; a counter-coup in July 1966 installed Lt-Col Yakubu Gowon. Gowon created 12 states in 1967. The Eastern Region declared secession as 'Biafra' under Lt-Col Odumegwu Ojukwu, and the civil war lasted from July 1967 to January 1970, ending with Gowon's policy of 'No victor, no vanquished' and the 3Rs (Reconciliation, Reconstruction, Rehabilitation).

material.heading: Unity institutions and the Fourth Republic
material.body: The National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) was established in 1973 to promote national unity. The federal character principle (1979 Constitution) ensures fair representation of states in public appointments. The Fourth Republic began on 29 May 1999 under the 1999 Constitution. National symbols include the green-white-green flag designed by Taiwo Akinkunmi, the national anthem 'Arise, O Compatriots' (adopted 1978) and the coat of arms with the motto 'Unity and Faith, Peace and Progress'.
keyPoints: Motto: Unity and Faith, Peace and Progress

topics.title: Culture, Values and Social Problems
topics.summary: Concept of culture, Nigerian cultural values, festivals, and challenges such as corruption and ethnicity.

material.heading: What is culture?
material.body: Culture is the total way of life of a people: their beliefs, values, norms, language, customs, arts and technology, learned and transmitted from one generation to the next. Material culture includes tangible items (tools, clothing, buildings); non-material culture includes beliefs, values, language and norms. Enculturation is learning one's own culture; acculturation is adopting traits from another culture through contact. Nigerian festivals include the Argungu fishing festival (Kebbi), Osun-Osogbo festival (Osun), Eyo festival (Lagos) and New Yam festival (Igbo land).
keyPoints: Culture is learned, shared and transmitted
Argungu: Kebbi; Osun-Osogbo: Osun; Eyo: Lagos

material.heading: Social problems and national development
material.body: Challenges to national development include corruption, ethnicity and tribalism, religious intolerance, insecurity and poor leadership. Anti-corruption agencies include the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC, 2003) and the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC, 2000). Good citizenship involves obeying laws, paying taxes, voting and respecting others' rights.
